title: French Advance: running the ...c5 siege as Black

difficulty.label: French player who wants the siege automatic, not remembered

objective.summary: You chose the French; 3.e5 is the most committal thing White can do to you. Run the siege in its canonical order — ...c5 at the base, ...Nc6, ...Qb6 — and keep every attacker pointed at d4 until White's defence costs them the rest of the board.

planClasses.label: Besiege d4 (...c5, ...Nc6, ...Qb6)
planClasses.description: The spine IS this plan: the pawn strike lands on move three and every following Black move adds an attacker to the base. The pack's central discipline is not resolving the tension — the siege works because it stands.

planClasses.label: Chip the head with ...f6 — later
planClasses.description: The second lever, correct only after the base fight settles and the king is safe. It appears in this pack once, as a classified mistake at the moment club players most often play it too soon.

planClasses.label: The cramped side's piece routes (...Nh6-f5, ...Bd7)
planClasses.description: Position-specific residue: with e6 blocking the c8 bishop and e5 denying f6 to the knight, Black's development is a routing problem — h6-f5 for the knight, d7 (and sometimes b5) for the bishop. The routes only make sense while the siege pins White down.

annotations: Immediately. The chain's base is d4, the c-pawn is your only piece of equipment that talks to it, and at your level this move is played in five of six French Advance games — it is the opening's reflex, and it should be yours.
White props the base and pays the standing price: the b1 knight has lost c3 forever. Remember that square — the knight's awkwardness is a debt your siege collects later.
Attacker two, on its natural square. Your development and your attack are the same moves in this structure — that is why the siege order is efficient and why deviating from it costs real tempi.
Defender two arrives. The count on d4 is level again, which is your cue for the next attacker, not for a trade.

The queen joins with a double purpose: third attacker on d4, first attacker on b2 — the pawn the c1 bishop must babysit, which keeps that bishop at home and White's queenside undeveloped. One move, two pins on White's agenda.

White's best answer: patience, preparing b4. This is YOUR decision point, and the honest options differ in kind — keep building with ...Nh6, close with ...c4, or release with ...cxd4. The spine keeps building; the checkpoint asks you to choose knowingly.

The Lputian move: the knight heads for f5, the only square from which it joins the siege, and it dares Bxh6 — a trade that hands you the bishop pair and the g-file for doubled pawns your structure can afford. The siege continues; nothing has been given back.

checkpoints.label: ...Qb6 — d4 and b2 both under pressure
...Nh6 — the last attacker takes the road to f5
You are past the authored line

deviations.note: 4...Qb6 before ...Nc6 is a real move order with one practical edge — it discourages White's Be3 setups a beat earlier — and one cost: the queen commits before White's system is known. Same siege, different door.

5...Bd7 — the Euwe Variation — solves the French bishop's whole life early, preparing ...Bb5 to trade it before the position decides it is bad. Slower on the siege by one move; permanently better for the worst piece. A legitimate different bargain.

5...Nge7 routes the knight to f5 via a square that does not invite Bxh6. It blocks the f8 bishop for a while, which is why the Nh6 route is the spine's choice — but both roads lead to f5, and choosing by taste is fine.

5...f6 chips the chain's head while the base fight is unresolved — the canonical impatience in this structure. exf6 hands White the e5 square and opens the position while your king still lives on e8 and your pieces point at d4, not at the centreline. The lever is real; this timing donates it.

6...c4 trades the siege for a bind: d4 is released, and in exchange the queenside is frozen with ...Na5-b3 as the long-term plan. A known strategy with a known cost — White's pieces turn kingside with free hands. Choosing it is a matter of style; drifting into it is a mistake. Play both and compare.

6...cxd4 releases the tension exactly when it was cheapest for White to live with: after cxd4 the c3 square returns to the b1 knight, b2 stops being loose the moment the rook comes to b1, and your siege has traded its standing threat for one open file. Keep the tension until resolving it wins something concrete.

feedbackClaims.text: After 3.e5 at the 1400/1600/1800 rating bands (Lichess blitz+rapid, 2024-01 through 2026-07), ...c5 is Black's choice in 83.5% of 9,215,262 games; the next most common try, ...Nc6, is 4.6%. The siege order this pack drills is the family's canon by an overwhelming margin.

In the Advance French, Black's developing moves and attacking moves are the same moves: ...c5, ...Nc6, ...Qb6 and the knight route to f5 all point at d4. That coincidence is why the cramped side is not worse — every tempo does double duty.

The c5/d4 tension is rent White pays every move: as long as it stands, White's pieces must stay coordinated around the base, and the moment they drift the capture wins material or squares. Resolving it early forgives the rent.
